'UI UX', 'UX/UI' and 'UI / UX' do NOT count for the title, H1, description, lead or kwCount. norm() lowercases, so 'EdTech' = 'edtech' in every check. proof.caseStudy: /case-studies/elia-wellness/ (content/case-studies/elia-wellness.md). This is the ONLY education or learning proof. No other edtech client, school, district, university, bootcamp, tutoring company or count may be claimed or implied.
supports: Elia Wellness is a holistic wellness initiative by the Sydney Adventist Church. It wanted a user-friendly learning management system (LMS) based on its popular book Live More.
Scope (quote exactly): 'idea to product, strategy, web app, mobile app and website.'
Audience: older adults, people over 50 (case wording: 'adults 50+', 'older adults', 'people over 50'), with 'very different comfort levels with technology'.

Challenge (paraphrase allowed): be intuitive; deliver meaningful, measurable wellness content, not just lessons to click through; go further than standard e-learning tools with gamification, social connection and interactive wellness tracking.

Approach: 'a human-centered approach focused on accessible, easy-to-navigate UI and UX', with 'responsive, mobile-friendly modules'. The platform is built around five experiences: a social feed to share and celebrate milestones; a wellness score across 7 dimensions (emotionally thriving, growth mindset, actively engaged, environmentally attuned, socially connected, physically energised, spiritually empowered); courses that course creators build from blocks (text, images, video and challenges); badges, where lessons unlock items in the learner's bucket list (seeing a sunrise, stretching day); progress monitoring (today's progress and weekly course stats).

Solution list: course creation for authors (lessons, modules and tutorials), performance tracking and interactive challenges, wellness dimensions and scoring, gamification such as badges, an integrated social feed. Also a desktop course builder for authors.

Devices: mobile screens (lesson with challenges, wellness score dashboard, personal growth questionnaire). The pre-course questionnaire 'works on tablets too, with large touch targets and simple rating scales.'

Results (quote exactly): '40% growth in user registrations' (growing from local origins to a worldwide wellness community) and '30+ boost in wellness scores among active users'. Frame both as the platform's reported results. Never attribute them to design alone.

Images that exist (reuse with the case-study alt text and captions only): /work/elia-wellness/cover.webp ('The Elia Wellness dashboard'), wellness-score.webp, course-editor.webp, badges.webp, course-progress.webp, course-builder.webp, mobile-screens.webp, tablet-questionnaire.webp, social-feed.webp.
doesNotSupport: Any school, K-12, district, college, university, bootcamp, corporate-training or tutoring client, and any count of edtech products, learners, institutions or courses.

Children or students as Elia's users. Elia's users are adults 50+, so COPPA and FERPA did NOT apply to Elia. Present COPPA and FERPA only as 'standards that apply' to products for children or schools, never as work we did or compliance we certified.

Compliance, certification or legal advice: we design consent, role and accessibility patterns. We do not certify WCAG, Section 508, ADA, COPPA or FERPA compliance, and we do not write VPATs or accessibility conformance reports.
Development or integration: LMS build, SCORM, xAPI, LTI, SIS or SSO integration, video hosting, content migration. The FAQ may say 'No' to these.
Curriculum, instructional design or course content production. The course builder lets Elia's course creators build lessons; we did not write the Live More course.
Usability testing or audits on Elia (not in its scope or body). Do not say 'tested with older adults'. Say the questionnaire was designed with large touch targets and simple rating scales.
Adaptive learning, AI tutoring, proctoring, assessment engines, live classrooms or video conferencing: none appear in the case study.
Expanding the scope words: 'strategy' stays 'strategy'; do not add 'research programme', 'branding' or 'design system'.
Leaderboard claims beyond the cover image alt ('a leaderboard' appears there once). Do not build a section around it.
proof.otherCaseStudies: Parents Connect (/case-studies/parents-connect/) is a parenting community with educational content and video episodes. It is NOT an edtech client. Use it at most once, as 'outside learning platforms, the same community patterns…', in the social-feed context. Skip it if the section runs over 70 words. No other case study is relevant.

outline.h2: Which learning screens do our edtech UI/UX design services cover?
outline.answerHint: Bold: our edtech UI/UX design services cover 6 parts of a learning platform that learners and course authors use, each drawn in every state (default, loading, empty, error and completed). One item per child, 1–2 sentences, one concrete example each.
points: Learner dashboard.: today's progress, next lesson, streaks or scores at a glance (Elia: 'Today's Progress' card and weekly course stats).
Course player.: video, text, images and challenges in one lesson view, with clear next and back.

Course builder and admin console.: course authors build lessons and modules from blocks (Elia: text, images, video and challenges). Link /services/web-app-design-services/ 'web app design services' (logged-in admin tools).
Progress tracking and badges.: gamification tied to lessons, not clicks (Elia: lessons unlock bucket-list items). Plain words 'learner badges'.
Learner onboarding.: sign-up, the first lesson and a pre-course questionnaire that sets a baseline (Elia: personal growth questionnaire on tablet).
Mobile learning app.: lessons and challenges on iOS and Android, with touch targets of 44×44 pt and 48×48 dp. Link /services/mobile-app-ui-ux-design-services/ 'mobile app UI UX design services'.

outline.h2: What makes edtech UX design different from other app design?
outline.answerHint: Bold: edtech UX design has to keep learners motivated over weeks of a learning platform, serve buyers who are not the users, and work for every age and ability. 4 cards, 1–2 sentences each.
points: Motivation over weeks, not one session: progress, badges and scores tied to lessons. Learner motivation comes from finishing the course, not points for clicks.
Several user groups on one platform: learners, course authors and administrators (and parents or teachers when children use it). Each gets its own dashboard and permissions.

Mixed ages and digital confidence: Elia served older adults with 'very different comfort levels with technology'. Large touch targets and simple rating scales on the pre-course questionnaire. Optional link /services/usability-testing-services/ 'usability testing services' with NO participant count.
Accessibility and privacy as buying criteria: public schools and universities buy against WCAG; children's products need parental consent (details in the standards section, no repeat).

outline.h2: How does our edtech UI/UX design process work?
outline.answerHint: Bold: our edtech UI/UX design services take a learning platform from discovery to developer handoff in 8–16 weeks (40–80 working days) and 5 steps. NO 'first designs in 1–2 weeks' clause. Use the parent hub's step names and days exactly, with edtech examples.
points: Discovery and product strategy (5–10 days): stakeholder workshops set the user groups (learners, course authors, administrators), the core learning loop and success metrics such as course completion. Link /blog/is-discovery-phase-worth-it/ 'what a discovery phase settles before screens'.
User research (5–15 days): researchers interview 5–8 learners per user group, and course authors, to find where onboarding, lessons and progress lose them.
Information architecture and flows (5–10 days): the team maps the course structure (courses, modules, lessons), the onboarding flow and the author's publishing flow.
Prototype and validation (10–20 days): 5 learners per round complete tasks in a clickable Figma prototype on Maze (parent hub figure; no usability-testing link in this sentence).

UI design and handoff (15–25 days): designers finish every screen state and hand annotated Figma files, design tokens and component specs to your engineers, with Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 level AA.

outline.h2: Edtech UI/UX design vs instructional design
outline.answerHint: Bold: edtech UI/UX design services decide how learners find, take and track courses on the learning platform; instructional design decides what each course teaches and in what order. Then the carrier sentence and 'The table compares both disciplines.' (table intro). Columns: Criterion | Edtech UI/UX design | Instructional design. Rows: Main question; Inputs (learner research, author workflows, analytics vs learning objectives and subject-matter experts); Outputs (flows, prototypes, UI screens and component specs in Figma vs course outlines, lesson scripts, assessments); Validation (prototype rounds with learners vs learning outcomes and assessment results); When to hire (learners get lost, drop out of the course player, authors struggle with the builder vs the content itself is unclear); Who does it ('Our senior design team, as on Elia Wellness' vs 'Your instructional designers or course authors; we do not write curriculum'). Compare disciplines, not vendors. This table also answers the 'lms design' (course design) confusion without targeting that term.
points: discipline comparison, no competitor names
honest scope: no curriculum

outline.h2: Which accessibility and privacy standards shape edtech UI/UX design services?
outline.format: list (plain-string items; the H2 must keep the word 'standards')
outline.answerHint: Bold: five accessibility and privacy standards shape edtech UI/UX design services for learning platforms, and each one changes what learners see on screen. Each item = one fact + its effect on screens + the primary link from externalSources. One closing sentence (in the answer or the last item): we design to these standards; legal compliance and certification stay with the product owner.
points: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 level AA: keyboard access, visible focus and 4.5:1 contrast for normal-size text across the learner dashboard and course player.

ADA Title II: the Department of Justice rule requires state and local governments, including public schools and universities, to make web content and mobile apps meet WCAG 2.1 level AA. An April 2026 interim final rule moved the compliance dates to April 26, 2027 (populations of 50,000 or more) and April 26, 2028 (smaller entities). Effect: platforms sold to public institutions are bought against WCAG. Fact-check the dates against ada.gov or the Federal Register; if unconfirmed, drop the dates and keep the WCAG 2.1 AA sentence.

Section 508: federal agencies must buy accessible information and communication technology, and the Revised 508 Standards incorporate WCAG 2.0 level AA. Effect: learning platforms sold to federal agencies need the same accessible patterns.

Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA): operators of services directed to children under 13 must get verifiable parental consent before collecting personal information. The FTC's amended rule took effect June 23, 2025, with compliance due April 22, 2026. Effect: sign-up and onboarding include a parent consent step and collect only what lessons need.

Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA): protects student education records at schools that receive US Department of Education funds. Effect: role-based views, so teachers and administrators see only the records they need, and grades never show on shared screens such as leaderboards.

outline.h2: FAQs about edtech UI/UX design services
outline.answerHint: Bold: these answers cover the 5 questions learning platform teams ask most before hiring edtech UI/UX design services.
points: see faqs[]

faqs.q: Have you designed a learning management system (LMS)?
faqs.a: Yes. For Elia Wellness, a wellness LMS for older adults based on the book Live More, we took the learning platform from idea to product across web app, mobile app and website. User registrations grew 40%. Link /case-studies/elia-wellness/. One project: do not pluralise, and do not say school or university.

faqs.q: Do you build the platform or integrate SCORM content?
faqs.a: No. Our designers deliver annotated Figma files, design tokens and component specs. Your engineers write the code and handle content standards such as SCORM and integrations with other systems. (Matches the hub's 'designers do not write code'.)

faqs.q: Can you redesign a learning platform that is already live?
faqs.a: Yes. Start with a UX audit of the live learning platform, $5,000–$15,000 over 2–3 weeks. It reviews onboarding, the course player and the course builder against usability heuristics and analytics, with a WCAG 2.2 level AA check. Its prioritized fix roadmap then scopes a design sprint. Link /services/ux-audit-services/.

faqs.q: Can you design an edtech product for children under 13?
faqs.a: Yes. The same 5-step process applies, and onboarding adds a COPPA parental consent step and collects only the data lessons need. Our published edtech work so far is Elia Wellness, which serves older adults, so we do not claim children's products as past work. Optional sibling link: /industries/startups/ 'startups UI UX design' for pre-launch teams.

faqs.q: Do you design the edtech website as well as the platform?
faqs.a: Yes. Edtech website design for the marketing site that leads learners into the platform runs through our UI UX web design practice (link /services/ui-ux-web-design/), and Elia Wellness's scope included its website. Do not add a website price unless it is the ui-ux-web-design hub's $25,000–$60,000 over 4–8 weeks, stated with that link.
